Richland County housing at a glance

Columbia, the state capital, anchors Richland County in the Midlands as its seat and largest community. Around it sit Cayce, Forest Acres, Arcadia Lakes, Blythewood, Eastover, Elgin and Irmo. The county had 416,147 residents in 2020, and health care leads local employment with 15.3% of jobs.

Whether a parcel lies in Eastover, Blythewood, Irmo or Columbia, one county Treasurer bills it. Typical sellers own an inherited house, a rental behind on tax or a home in poor shape, and each situation calls for its own tax step before closing.

Where to pay and who to call

Assessor2020 Hampton Street, Suite 2058, Columbia, SC 29204; mail to P.O. Box 192, Columbia, SC 29202803-576-2640; assessoroffice@richlandcountysc.gov

Payment is accepted online, at the counter or through the mail, and a monthly plan is available. Customer service, planned payments and tax sale questions each have their own Treasurer email address.

Due dates and penalties

The penalty-free window closes January 15 (S.C. Code 12-45-70). Late charges under 12-45-180 then run 3%, followed by 7% more ahead of February 2 and 5% more ahead of March 17.

Penalties are waived when ownership changed during the tax year and the buyer never received the notice on time. If your closing fits that pattern, say so to the Treasurer's office.

The annual tax sale

Each fall the county auctions delinquent parcels by sealed bid at the Richland County Township Auditorium, 1703 Taylor Street, Columbia. The top bidder gets the property as is, paying cash. An owner who wants a parcel pulled must get cash or a certified cashier's check to the Treasurer by the announced cutoff. Personal, company and escrow checks don't count.

  • Registration for bidders is online only and costs $50.00.
  • Bidding opens at the sum of delinquent taxes, sale costs and current year taxes.
  • A winner who doesn't pay owes $500 per bid and court costs.
  • Title passes without warranty, and the county may cancel a sale before the deed issues.

Because the schedule changes yearly, ask the Treasurer for current dates.

How often the county reassesses

Every five years the Assessor revalues the whole county, following S.C. Code 12-43-217. The next year is a question for 803-576-2640. Notice is owed when a value or classification shifts by $1,000 or more, and an ordinance can hold off new values for one tax year at most.

Beyond values, that office deals with rollback taxes on farmland that changes use, HOA properties, active military residential exemptions and deed sale records. Multiple-lot and builder or developer discounts, commercial ATI exemptions and mailing address changes are on its list as well, so let it know when you sell or move.

How to appeal your assessment

Your written objection must reach the Assessor within 90 days of the date on the reassessment notice. In a year with no notice, the first penalty date on the tax bill is the cutoff. Online filers follow whichever date comes first.

  1. Go through the county's Appeal Your Assessment portal, or write a letter.
  2. Attach papers that challenge the assessed value or classification.
  3. A representative filing on your behalf needs a power of attorney on SC DOR Form SC2848.
  4. An LLC or similar owner adds its Articles of Organization or Operating Agreement.

Disputes between taxpayer and Assessor go to a Board of Assessment Appeals. Paper filings can be sent to the Assessor's street address or P.O. Box.

Legal residence and the 4% rate

A home that meets the residency and ownership tests drops from the 6% ratio to 4%. The rate under S.C. Code 12-43-220 reaches the house and as many as five contiguous acres, and leasing the house more than 72 days in a calendar year forfeits it.

Anyone who loses eligibility and keeps quiet past six months risks a charge equal to the tax paid, plus 0.5% interest monthly, with a floor of $30.

Landlords and heirs who live elsewhere should plan on 6%. The same section treats active-duty residents with South Carolina duty stations as domiciled here.

Selling when you owe tax

Begin with a payoff number from the Treasurer so you know what will leave your proceeds. Closing pays the tax, and Cash Home Buyers will purchase the house in its present state, repairs not required.

  • Treasurer, 803-576-2250: current bill and tax sale questions.
  • Assessor, 803-576-2640: rate, value and appeals.
  • Deed recording: $1.85 per $500 of value, split $1.30 state and $0.55 county (S.C. Code 12-24-10), with deeds in lieu of foreclosure exempt.

Cash also avoids the lender appraisal and a buyer's repair list, which fits a house in poor condition or an estate in a hurry.

Payment plans in more detail

Short of cash on January 15? Ask the Treasurer about the monthly plan. It spreads out the payments without protecting you: until the full amount is in, penalties and collection steps can continue. Think of it as a bridge to a sale more than a way to keep a house you can't afford.

Selling while on a plan? Tell the title company up front. The payoff is the leftover balance plus any penalties that have built up, and the Treasurer can supply it. The planned-payments email address works for written questions about your account.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

A sensible order for a quick sale

First, the Treasurer: confirm the balance, which years are open and whether the parcel is headed for the fall sale. Second, the Assessor: which rate applies and whether a reassessment is near. Third, pass both answers to the title company with your target closing date.

A closing ahead of the fall sale keeps the property out of the auction altogether. Auction buyers get title without warranty and the county can cancel a sale, so no owner should count on that route. Selling first is cleaner.

Keep a written record of every call. Note the date, the person you spoke with and the figure you were given, since payoff amounts change as penalty dates pass and you may need to show where a number came from.

Photo ID and the property address are the basics at the Hampton Street office. Executors and agents should add proof of authority, and an LLC owner should have its founding papers handy.

Inherited and rental houses

An inherited house may hold several years of tax and a classification that no longer fits. Heirs who live elsewhere face the 6% rate, and the balance may include old penalties. Ask the Treasurer for a full payoff and set it beside what a buyer will pay.

Landlords with a rental in arrears face the same arithmetic. Tax is paid from the proceeds, so the question is whether the price covers the balance with margin. A cash buyer can quote a number fast, since no lender appraisal is involved.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Richland County tax deadline?

Pay by January 15 to avoid penalties. A 3% charge starts after that date.

Where is the Richland County Treasurer?

At 2020 Hampton Street, Columbia, SC 29204. Call 803-576-2250 during weekday hours of 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m.

How do I appeal my Richland County assessment?

Write to the Assessor within 90 days of the reassessment notice, or use the online portal. Someone filing for you needs Form SC2848.

Can I pay Richland County tax in installments?

Yes, through the Treasurer's monthly plan, though collection steps go on until the full amount is paid.

Can I sell a Richland County house with unpaid property tax?

Yes. Closing pays the tax from your proceeds, and Cash Home Buyers can buy the house in its current condition.

Greenville County at a glance

No South Carolina county has more residents than Greenville: 525,534 in 2020, with 583,125 estimated for 2025. The county seat is the city of Greenville. Fountain Inn, Greer, Mauldin, Simpsonville and Travelers Rest are the remaining cities, and big unincorporated areas like Taylors, Berea and Wade Hampton sit outside all of them.

The housing is a mix of eras: turn-of-the-century houses, mill villages, postwar subdivisions and brand-new builds. Age drives a buyer's repair estimate, and a Travelers Rest house near the mountains attracts a different crowd than a Mauldin house by the interstate, even though one set of county offices taxes both.

Due dates and penalties

Greenville County wants real property tax paid by January 15. Notices typically mail near the end of October. After the deadline, penalties build in steps under S.C. Code 12-45-180.

DatePenalty added to the bill
January 15None, last day to pay
January 163 percent
February 2Further 7 percent
March 17Further 5 percent plus a $15.00 execution cost

Penalty relief is rare. The Tax Collector will take charges off only if you can show the county itself made a mistake. Visit the South Building, Suite 1100-S, or phone 864.467.7050. Payment can be made at the counter, by mail or on the web, and most payments show as posted within three to five business days.

The lien rides with the parcel, never with a particular owner. When a house closes with this year's tax still open, the escrow agent takes the amount out of the seller's proceeds.

What a sale does to the assessment

Nearly every sale is an assessable transfer of interest. Real Property Services then appraises the house again, drops the 15 percent limit on yearly increases, and for a point-of-sale reassessment values it as of December 31 of the transfer year. Expect the buyer's fresh notice a year later.

The January 1 owner of record gets the bill. If the deed moves after that date, that year's bill lists both the former and the incoming owner, and the next year's bill lists only the new one.

  • A home the owner lives in qualifies for the 4 percent legal residence assessment and a credit that wipes out the school operating tax. The form needs a handwritten original signature and has to be delivered by hand or postmarked by January 15. Online filing is not an option.
  • A landlord-buyer gets neither benefit, and that first bill may land well above the one you paid.
  • Transfers made in the prior year have until January 30 to claim the 25 percent exemption.

Pass this along to your buyer early. For anything unclear, call Real Property Services at 864.467.7300.

How to appeal your assessment

Put any appeal on paper. Your assessment notice prints the cutoff date. If you never got a notice, plan on January 15, shifting to the next working day when it falls on a weekend or holiday. S.C. Code 12-60-2510 gives 90 days after mailing when the notice increased value by $1,000 or more.

  1. Mail a letter of objection that includes the tax map number, why you disagree and the value you think is right. Fax and email do not count, and the postmark settles timeliness.
  2. A certified appraiser looks at each appeal filed on time. The assessor then mails you the outcome.
  3. If you disagree, take it to the County Board of Assessment Appeals by protesting within 30 days of the decision notice.
  4. If the Board rules against you in writing, another 30 days opens for the Administrative Law Judge Division.

The address is Real Property Services, Greenville County Square, Suite 1000. Late summer and early fall are when new-construction notices tend to go out.

When taxes go unpaid

March 17 ends the grace and makes the bill delinquent, so the Tax Collector sends an execution notice. Thirty days after that mailing, an unpaid account gets a Notice of Seizure sent certified with restricted delivery.

The auction itself takes place at the Greenville Convention Center on Exposition Drive, following three weekly advertisements. Bidding opens at the total of delinquent tax, penalties and costs plus the current year's tax.

Redemption stays open for 12 months. The former owner, a grantee, or a creditor holding a mortgage or judgment may pay and take the property back, with interest on the bid at 3 percent for months one to three, 6 percent for months four to six, 9 percent for months seven to nine and 12 percent for months ten to twelve. Without redemption, the winning bidder gets a tax deed passing only whatever interest the county held, with no warranty behind it.

Recording the deed

The Register of Deeds is in Suite S-2100 at Greenville County Square, 301 University Ridge. Weekday hours run 8:30 am to 5:00 pm, though the staff would like you through the door by 4:30 pm.

The deed fee comes from S.C. Code Title 12, Chapter 24: $1.85 on every $500 of value or fraction of it. The state keeps $1.30 and the county keeps $0.55. Foreclosure-related deeds to the lender and some family partnership or trust transfers are exempt.

In a normal closing the escrow firm drafts the deed and subtracts the fee from the funds it holds. Filing by mail on your own means enclosing a note with your telephone number, a prepaid return envelope and a check payable to Greenville County.

Selling with taxes owed

Unpaid tax makes a sale slower, not impossible. Here is how it usually plays out.

  1. Ring the Tax Collector, 864.467.7050, for the amount needed to clear the parcel. After March 17, make sure the figure carries penalties and the execution cost.
  2. Give the number to whoever runs your closing. It becomes a line item on the settlement statement.
  3. Funds go to the county out of your sale proceeds when the deed records, so no separate payment is needed from you.

Closing before an auction is nearly always smarter. Escrow wipes out the debt at once, and neither redemption interest nor a tax deed ever enters the picture.

Bring your deed or tax map number, the newest bill and a photo ID to the counter. If you inherited the home, estate documents usually have to be ready before a closing date gets picked.

With no lender involved, a cash sale has no appraisal wait and no repair negotiation. Title work and the payoff figure set the pace, and the house stays as you left it.

Frequently asked questions

What is the last day to pay Greenville County real estate tax without a penalty?

January 15. Starting January 16 the bill grows by 3 percent, then 7 percent more on February 2, then 5 percent more along with a $15.00 execution cost on March 17.

Is it possible to close on a Greenville County home that still owes tax?

It is. The balance is deducted from what you receive at the closing table, so nothing needs to be paid beforehand. A cash deal can close the same way.

Where do I send an assessment objection in Greenville County?

To Real Property Services at Greenville County Square, Suite 1000, phone 864.467.7300. Write it out, and remember the postmark is what counts.

Will my buyer pay more than I did?

Quite possibly. The sale usually triggers a fresh valuation and ends the 15 percent cap, and a buyer who will not live there misses the 4 percent legal residence rate.

What is the redemption window after a Greenville County tax auction?

It lasts 12 months from the auction date. To get the property back, the owner, a grantee or a mortgage or judgment creditor pays the tax, penalties and costs plus interest on the bid, which climbs each quarter.

Lexington County in brief

The Columbia metro area includes Lexington County, in the Midlands, where Lake Murray accounts for much of the water. Lexington, the seat and largest community, had 23,568 residents in 2020. Countywide, people numbered 262,391 in 2010 and 293,991 in 2020, with 317,588 estimated for 2025.

New building clusters on the eastern and northeastern side, closest to Columbia. A lake-area house, a subdivision near Irmo and a rural parcel near Gilbert share a county but move on different timelines. Rapid growth usually lifts assessed values at the next reassessment, so someone who bought a few years back may find the bill larger than they budgeted. For a house near Lake Murray or the Saluda, Broad and Congaree rivers, look into drainage and flood questions yourself before a buyer's inspector raises them.

Offices and contact details

Collection, valuation and exemptions are split three ways: Treasurer, Assessor and Auditor.

You can pay at the counter, on the web at lex-co.sc.gov, by check to PO Box 604397, Charlotte, NC 28260-4397, or at the night deposit box outside the County Administration Building. Card payments add convenience fees.

Due dates and penalties

Notices for real property go out after October 1 to the owner of record. Pay the whole bill by the next January 15. A payment with a later postmark gathers penalties on January 16, February 2 and March 17.

Those penalties are 3 percent, 7 percent more and 5 percent more, per S.C. Code 12-45-180. Penalties continue to build during a penalty appeal unless you pay in full, and the county gives back what you paid if the appeal is granted. Send penalty appeals to the Treasurer in writing, and call (803) 785-8217 for instructions.

Mail only checks, and send them early, since the postmark is what counts. If the mail feels risky near the deadline, use the night deposit box or the online payment page instead.

Installment plan

Real property that is not paid through escrow is eligible for the county's installment program. Participants pay five advance installments set from the prior year's tax, and November 15 is when the leftover balance is billed.

You re-enroll yearly, and dropping out takes written consent. If you are enrolled and plan to sell, ask the Treasurer before closing how the plan will be handled. A forgotten enrollment is a frequent loose end after a house changes hands.

How to appeal your assessment

Your written appeal reaches the Assessor within 90 days of the notice date. Without a notice, the county's FAQ points to a January 1 through January 15 window the next year.

Market value is what an appeal tests. Calling the tax bill too large is not a valid ground. An appeal still pending on December 31 means billing at no less than 80 percent of assessed value, and payment is still owed January 15. After the ruling, interest applies either way: a refund to you or a balance owed.

A Board of Assessment Appeals with nine members, chosen by County Council, hears cases when asked, in the Council Chambers of the County Administration Building, and agendas appear on the county meeting portal. State rules entitle owners to notice of a rise of $1,000 or more. The county reappraised in 2015 and 2020, a five-year rhythm, and the Assessor can tell you the next date.

What changes when a house sells

Whatever the seller still owes for the year comes out of the proceeds at closing. The buyer files a separate application for the 4 percent legal residence ratio, due before the first penalty date of the year it is first claimed.

These are the loose ends that most often trip up Lexington County sellers:

  • A rental over the 72-day limit that was taxed at 6 percent.
  • An installment plan left active after the sale.
  • A bill that went to a former address because the Assessor was never told about the move.
  • A lake or older-neighborhood house that needs roof, septic or foundation work before a lender will finance the buyer.

If back tax and repairs both block a sale, selling as-is for cash lets the title company pay the county out of your proceeds. For the payoff and the tax sale schedule, call the Delinquent Tax Department at (803) 785-8345.

Steps before you list

A short routine keeps the sale on track.

  1. See the Treasurer first: is the account paid, or in the installment plan? Get written instructions for leaving the plan if you are in it.
  2. Call the Auditor to find out whether a homestead exemption is on the account, and report the pending sale.
  3. Have the Assessor fix your mailing address and tell you whether rental use put the legal residence ratio at risk.
  4. If any bill has gone past due, ask the Delinquent Tax Department for a payoff.

Carry the deed or parcel number, your latest bill and a photo ID. Because the penalty dates are January 16, February 2 and March 17, an early quote goes stale, so request a new number once you have a closing date.

With a cash buyer there is no loan appraisal to wait for. Title work and the payoff set the pace instead, and you can start both the day you decide to sell.

Legal residence ratio and rental use

A house you live in is taxed on a 4 percent ratio, while other property is taxed on 6 percent. The 72-day rental limit is the line to watch: a home rented for more than 72 days in a calendar year loses the lower ratio. If you rented the house out at any point before selling, ask the Assessor how that affects the account.

The same ratio matters to your buyer. Someone who closes late in the year and does not file before the first penalty date pays at 6 percent for that year, so a note to your buyer about the deadline helps them as much as it helps you.

Closing-day tax questions

Three questions are worth settling before you sign. First, how much is still owed, and through what date does that figure hold? Second, has the Auditor heard about the sale, so the homestead exemption can come off? Third, does the Assessor have the buyer's mailing address for next year's notice? Your title company covers the first, and the other two are on you.

When a bill is already past due, the Delinquent Tax Department is the office to call. It can give you the amount and tell you where the account stands in the process.

When is Lexington County property tax due?

The whole amount is owed by January 15 of the year following the tax year, and penalties start on January 16.

Where is the Lexington County Treasurer's office?

212 South Lake Drive, Suite 101, Lexington, SC 29072. The phone is (803) 785-8217, and hours are Monday to Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

How long do I have to appeal a Lexington County assessment?

Ninety days from the date on the notice. If none came, the county's guidance is to appeal between January 1 and January 15 of the next year.

Does Lexington County have an installment plan?

Yes, if the property is not paid through escrow. Five advance payments are based on last year's tax, with the remainder billed by November 15.

Can I sell a Lexington County house with unpaid property tax?

Yes, and closing takes care of it, since the title company pays the balance from your proceeds. The Delinquent Tax Department, (803) 785-8345, can quote the current amount.

Reassessment and the legal residence rate

  • Legal residence status, the 4 percent assessment, must be applied for between January 1 and January 15.

  • The $50,000 homestead deduction covers owners 65 or older, the blind, the disabled and surviving spouses. First-time applicants file in person at the Auditor's Office, 843-915-5051.

How to appeal your assessment

Ask for a conference in writing within 90 days of the assessment notice. In a year with no notice, you can appeal whenever you like, and an appeal filed before the first penalty date counts for that tax year.

The letter should give your name, the Map-Block-Parcel number, the value you think is correct and why. The legal basis is S.C. Code 12-60-2510. When agricultural land changes use, roll-back taxes apply for the year of change and the four years before.

Delinquent taxes and the tax sale

On March 17 real property taxes become delinquent. Notices follow around April 1, certified notices come roughly 30 days after that, and levy notices are posted at delinquent properties, usually sometime from May through October.

Three Thursdays in a row carry the sale advertisement. After the sale, you have 12 months to redeem. The Delinquent Tax Office, 1301 Second Avenue in Conway, takes calls at (843) 915-5472 and keeps weekday hours of 8 am to 5 pm. Look for the sale date and location in a November newspaper ad.

When the property changes hands, state and county recording tax on the deed is $1.85 per $500 of value, set by Title 12, Chapter 24.

Flood-prone houses

Water covers about 9 percent of the county, and the Waccamaw and Pee Dee rivers and the Intracoastal Waterway all run through it. The county's flood plan says Hurricane Florence damaged more than 2,000 buildings and closed more than 460 roads. Bucksport, Longs, Red Bluff and Socastee are named as target communities.

Flood maps matter at sale time. In Socastee, fewer than 20 percent of damaged buildings (96 of 565) sat inside the Special Flood Hazard Area on the maps in effect. Check the flood zone and the insurance claim history for your house before you list it. If the house is damaged or flood-prone, a buyer who pays cash and takes it as-is can purchase it without asking you to rebuild.

Selling when you live elsewhere or owe tax

Living out of state need not slow you down, because nearly every step works over the phone. The Treasurer, 843-428-2126, quotes a payoff that rises at each penalty date. The Auditor, 843-915-5051, can say whether a homestead deduction sits on the account, and the Assessor can explain your legal residence rate.

Then read the recorded deed and confirm it carries the seller's name. A unit passed down in the family generally needs the estate settled first. The county is paid from your proceeds by the title company at the closing table.

A cash buyer who takes the property as it stands removes repairs, showings and loan delays. Two questions are worth raising early with the Assessor: whether roll-back taxes apply to farmland, and whether a change of use has been reported.

Keep the Treasurer's receipt, your closing statement and the deed copy together. The following year's bill will go to the new owner of record, so the Assessor needs your forwarding address if you are still receiving mail for the old one.

Before you list: a short checklist

  1. Look up your account with the Treasurer and note the balance and the date it was quoted.
  2. Confirm the legal residence rate and any homestead deduction are on file. If they are not, ask the Assessor and the Auditor how a sale affects them.
  3. Pull the recorded deed and compare names, the tax map number and the Map-Block-Parcel number.
  4. Check flood zone status and past insurance claims, especially near Socastee or Bucksport.
  5. Ask whether any use changes were reported to the Assessor in the last six months.

A sale is usually the event that triggers a fresh valuation and lifts the 15 percent cap, so the next owner's bill may look quite different from yours. Telling your buyer about that early prevents an unpleasant surprise after closing.

Frequently asked questions

What is the payment deadline for real property in Horry County?

January 15, with notices mailed on October 1. Penalties kick in on January 16, February 2 and March 17.

Is there an installment option in Horry County?

Yes, for real property when your application arrives before January 15. Five payments of 16.67 percent of last year's tax run from February through October, and the rest is billed by November 15.

When can I apply for the 4 percent rate in Horry County?

File in that window, January 1 to January 15. The home must be yours, and your primary residence, on January 1.

What is the redemption period after an Horry County tax sale?

One year, counted from the day of the sale. Whoever owned the house, a lender or a grantee can recover it by paying the taxes and costs of the sale.

Do Horry County homes face flood risk?

Some do. The county's plan singles out Bucksport, Longs, Red Bluff and Socastee, so look up the flood zone and insurance history before listing.

Spartanburg County in brief

In the far northwest of South Carolina, against the North Carolina border, Spartanburg County covers 819.74 square miles, with 808.34 of them land. Its seat and largest community is the city of Spartanburg. Greer, Duncan, Boiling Springs, Inman, Landrum and Woodruff ring the city, which means a seller might hold a downtown bungalow, a house in a subdivision off the interstate, or a rural lot.

Millage is decided locally every year, so ask about your own parcel rather than borrowing a neighbor's bill. The older neighborhoods, including Hampton Heights and the Beaumont Mill village, take in a designated local historic district. Owners there should phone the city before planning work on the outside of the house.

Damp, hot summers and 50 to 51 inches of rain annually wear on roofs, gutters and crawl spaces. When repairs have been put off for years, selling as-is can beat paying for all of them first.

Offices and contacts

Three offices share the job: the Assessor values property and hears appeals, and the Treasurer and the Delinquent Tax Office take payment. Drop by the Administration Building at 366 N Church Street, Spartanburg, on weekdays from 8 AM until 5 PM. Delinquent taxes are handled at 864-596-2597 or P.O. Box 3060, Spartanburg, SC 29304.

Take your parcel number and newest notice along. Counter staff can say where your file sits, and a few minutes in person often settles what a letter would take days to answer.

Due dates and penalties

Payment is accepted from September 30 until January 15 after assessment. Late charges build in three steps under the county's rules and S.C. Code 12-45-180.

If the bill is unpaid byPenalty addedRunning total

By March 17 the bill is delinquent, and a tax execution goes from the Treasurer to the Tax Collector. Reappraisal and the 15% cap

The latest reappraisal reset values to market conditions on December 31, 2022, and the 2023 bills used those numbers. More than 180,567 notices went into the mail by September 2023.

  • A reappraisal can lift your value by at most 15%, except for new or improved structures, a sale or a transfer of interest.
  • A notice of value is never a tax bill.
  • State law calls for reappraisal every five years, and the Assessor can name the next date.

Don't assume the seller's old bill carries over. A recent sale can strip the cap's protection from the new owner, which means a buyer should budget from the new value.

How to appeal your assessment

Put your objection in writing and get it to the Assessor inside 90 days of the notice's mailing date. Five stages follow.

  1. Request a meeting in writing. If the Assessor sides with you, the value changes and that is the end of it.
  2. If not, attend the conference, because skipping it forfeits any further appeal that year.
  3. Send a written protest stating your facts, legal grounds and the value you believe is right.
  4. A written reply comes from the Assessor in roughly 30 days, after which you have 30 days to go to the County Board of Assessment Appeals.
  5. Thirty days after the Board rules, you may ask for a contested case at the Administrative Law Court.

In a year with no reappraisal notice, the filing date picks the tax year: before January 15 and it covers the current year, on or after and it covers the next. An appeal never postpones payment. If you ask in writing before December 31, you can be billed on at least 80% of the protested value while the case is pending. Comparable market sales are good evidence; forced, distressed and foreclosure sales generally are not.

If the tax goes unpaid

Enforcement climbs in stages, from an execution notice to a notice of seizure and finally a public auction. Thirty days of silence after the execution notice brings the notice of seizure, sent certified with restricted delivery. After that the property is advertised once a week for three weeks and then sold.

For 12 months after the sale, the owner, the owner's grantee, or a mortgage or judgment creditor can buy the property back. Interest on the bid rises with time after the sale: 3% if you redeem in months one to three, 6% in months four to six, 9% in months seven to nine and 12% in months ten to twelve. If no one redeems, the Tax Collector issues a tax deed. It has no warranty and passes only the county's interest. A top bidder who fails to pay owes $500 per property.

Under 12-51-120, the owner must get a certified mailing 45 to 20 days ahead of the redemption deadline.

Common slip-ups

Three mistakes show up again and again. The first is assuming a mailed notice settles anything: a reappraisal notice is only an announcement, and the real bill arrives later. The second is missing the conference after you file an objection, which ends your appeal for that year. The third is waiting until March 17 to learn the payoff, by which point the stacked penalties have reached 15% and the account has gone to the Tax Collector.

A smaller one is trusting an old figure. Millage changes every year, and a buyer who budgets from the seller's last bill can be caught short. If you are on either side of a sale, ask the Assessor for the current value and the Treasurer for the current payoff on the day you talk.

Notes for heirs and landlords

Heirs often inherit a tax problem along with the house. Check whether the bills were mailed to a relative who has died, because a notice that went to the wrong person doesn't stop the penalties, though state law does provide for waivers when a transfer left the owner uninformed. Landlords should remember that the 15% cap doesn't shield a property after it sells, so rent projections for a new owner need current numbers.

If the house is vacant, visit it regularly. Open mail piles up, and a seizure notice sent by certified mail can sit unclaimed. Giving the Treasurer a current address now is cheaper than learning about a tax sale after it is advertised.

What to bring and what to expect

Bring the tax bill, the parcel number, any execution notice and a photo ID when you visit an office. If the property is inherited, add whatever shows who has authority to sign. For an appeal, add recent sales of similar homes nearby, since comparable market sales count as evidence. Keep a copy of every paper you file, along with the date.

Expect a few steps, not one. The Treasurer quotes the payoff, the closing attorney or title company checks the record, and the deed is recorded after funds move. Setting aside a few days for each step keeps the schedule realistic.

Selling with taxes owed

The seller's proceeds normally cover the unpaid balance and penalties at the table. State code 12-45-140 lets the county auditor apportion tax when ownership transfers, and the closing attorney can show how the current year was split.

  • Locate the tax bill and any execution notice first.
  • Get the Treasurer's payoff, penalties included.
  • A bill mailed to a former owner may qualify for a waiver under 12-45-180.
  • A cash buyer should hear immediately if a tax sale clock is running.

When are Spartanburg County property taxes due?

Payment opens September 30 and stays penalty-free to January 15. A 3% penalty begins January 16, with 7% more on February 2 and 5% more on March 17, reaching 15%.

How long do I have to appeal my Spartanburg County assessment?

You have 90 days after the Assessor mails the notice, and the objection must be written. The tax due date stays put.

Can I get my Spartanburg County house back after a tax sale?

Yes, for a year after the sale. You pay taxes, penalties and costs plus 3%, 6%, 9% or 12% interest, depending on the month you redeem. A grantee or a mortgage or judgment creditor can redeem too.

Will the 15% reappraisal cap apply after I sell?

Often not. Sold property, an assessable transfer or new or improved structures fall outside the cap, so the buyer's bill follows the new value.

Yes. Your proceeds usually clear the balance at closing. Request a payoff that includes penalties from the Treasurer, and tell any buyer if a tax sale is near.

After a reassessment, state law requires cities to reset their rates to stay revenue neutral, and the Auditor supplies the rollback figure. Questions about the process go to the reassessment hotline at (843) 958-4144.

Challenges have three tiers. An objection is an informal review. A protest is a formal one. Hold on to the Treasurer's last receipt as well. It shows the address the county has on record, which is a quick way to spot an outdated mailing address before closing day.

Who bills and collects property tax

Three desks handle one tax bill. Real Property Services puts values on land and buildings. The Auditor posts the calendar and takes business personal property returns. The Treasurer takes the money, then splits it among the county, the towns, the school districts and the special taxing districts.

Due dates and penalties

Berkeley bills real estate after the tax year ends. Notices go out in October, and payment is due on January 15 of the next year. A January 15 that lands on a weekend or holiday rolls forward to the next business day. For mail, only the postmark matters: stamped on or before the due date means on time.

From January 16 the penalties start piling on. The statute adds 3 percent at the start, another 7 percent from February 2, and a final 5 percent from March 17. Once March 17 is behind you, the treasurer may issue an execution for the unpaid tax, the penalties and the costs.

It organizes and conducts the auctions of land and mobile homes, with notices running in the Post and Courier. After an auction it researches title and prepares the deed.

A completed auction is not always the end. The owner, a grantee, or a mortgage or judgment creditor can redeem within twelve months of the sale. Interest on the winning bid starts at 3 percent for the first quarter and rises to 12 percent by the fourth, so each quarter of delay costs more.

How reassessment and appeals work

Every property in South Carolina is reappraised on a five-year rhythm. Berkeley's program years are 1981, 1985, 1999, 2004, 2009, 2014, 2019 and 2024. Appraisers aim for fair market value, and millage for each taxing body comes out of its budget divided by the combined assessments.

Current recipients stay put unless something changes, and the breakdown shows on each yearly bill. That same office looks at agricultural use, rollback taxes, builder and HOA classifications, and the Commercial ATI exemption.

Write down the dates when a deed changed names, because ownership changes are what trigger new legal residence applications.

If the property includes acreage, ask Real Property how the land is classified. Agricultural use can bring rollback taxes when the use changes, and a buyer's lender or attorney will ask about it. When York County taxes are due

The payment window opens September 30 and stays penalty-free through the following January 15. One notice is printed for each parcel, addressed to the person who held title on January 1. Installments are off the table, since state law doesn't authorize them, which means co-owners have to settle between themselves how to cover the single bill. Lenders can get their own copy by asking the county in writing.

Once January 15 passes, penalties follow S.C. Code 12-45-180. The tax collector can quote an exact payoff, so rely on that rather than doing the arithmetic.

A penalty gets forgiven only if there is direct proof the county made a mistake, for instance one linked to a change of ownership.

Tax notices after you buy or sell

A buyer's first bill may show the seller's name, since January 1 ownership controls. The county reassigns it to the new owner a year later. Call the assessor first. Errors such as wrong acreage or a missing 4 percent status often get corrected with no formal appeal. When a call doesn't solve it, send a written objection to the assessor no later than 90 days after the notice was mailed.

Every October or November. The date appears on the county website ahead of time, and The Herald runs the property list weekly for three weeks beforehand.

Summerville, Ladson and Lincolnville each cross into a neighboring county, so a mailing address near a town line may point to the wrong county. Find the parcel's tax map number first, then look for the bill.

Age matters in this housing stock. A home near the Summerville Historic District will need different repairs from a subdivision house built in the last twenty years, and the inspection report usually drives the buyer's requests.

Due dates and penalties

The deadline for real property tax is January 15, with penalties starting the next day. Payment season opens September 30, and bills have gone out in mid October in earlier years. Section 12-45-180 lets the penalties stack.

After March 16, an unpaid bill is handed to the Delinquent Tax Office with the 15 percent penalty already attached. One narrow exception exists. When ownership changed mid-year and the notice reached only the previous owner, the treasurer shall waive penalties for a new owner who got no timely notice. Treat that as a long shot, and after any purchase or sale, verify who the bill is addressed to.

Payment works online through the county taxes portal, at the St. George or Summerville Treasurer's offices, or by mail in the return envelope. A bill that has not shown up by November 10 is a reason to phone the Assessor's Office at (843) 832-0162 and check the mailing address.

Which office handles what

Each office has a distinct task: the Assessor sets the value, the Auditor figures the bill, and the Treasurer takes the payment.

  • Assessor and legal residence: (843) 832-0162, with offices in St. George and Summerville. The St. George address is 201 Johnston Street, St. George, SC 29477.

What a sale does to the assessment

A sale usually brings a new appraisal. The Property Tax Reform Act of 2006 made most transfers assessable, which means the county values the property at market as of December 31 of the year it sold. Expect the next owner's bill to look different from yours.

Owner-occupied homes, manufactured homes among them, qualify for the 4 percent legal residence rate, one per owner. Report a change of owner, mailing address or use to the Assessor inside six months. Buyers need to wait for the deed to be recorded with the Register of Deeds before applying, or the application may be returned.

Mobile homes follow separate rules. Registration is due within 15 days of buying one in the county or moving one here. A moving permit lasts 30 days and requires back taxes to be paid first. When ownership changes, a name change permit is needed, and fines of up to $200 may apply. Call the Assessor at (843) 832-0162.

Farmland comes with a catch. Changing its use triggers a rollback of up to three years of tax savings, and the bill can land on whoever changes the use, which may be the new owner. The Assessor's site has a request form for a rollback estimate.

How to challenge your assessment

Send the assessor a written objection no later than 90 days after the notice goes in the mail. That is the rule in Section 12-60-2510 of the state code, and it reaches disputes about fair market value, special use value, the assessment ratio and the assessment as a whole.

A notice is required whenever fair market value climbs $1,000 or more and when a property is first assessed, usually by July 1. During a countywide reassessment, notices are due by October 1. With no notice at all, a written appeal is still possible at any time. Filed before the first penalty date, it covers that year; filed on or after, it covers the next. The Assessor can supply the current form.

Collection costs when taxes go unpaid

Fees climb through the year. In the most recent cycle the county added $35 to real property bills and $45 to mobile home bills in spring, a $35 posting fee in early summer and an $80 advertising charge by late October. Cards carry a 2.95 percent convenience fee and cannot be used to redeem property sold at a tax sale.

A few calls early save trouble later. Ask the Assessor whether your legal residence application is on file and whether any mobile home permits are open. Keep a short list of what you learn: who you spoke to, the date and the figure they gave. Your closing agent will want the same details, and buyers sometimes ask whether the property's classification will change after the sale. The honest answer, for most sales in Dorchester County, is that it will be reappraised at market value as of December 31 of the sale year.

Selling a Dorchester County house with unpaid tax

A tax balance does not prevent a sale, though the tax, penalties and any collection fees all have to be paid off. Because fees change by date, a current payoff from the Delinquent Tax Office is the number to work from.

  2. Ask your closing agent how the payoff will be sent.

The Assessor's Office, at (843) 832-0162. You can apply online or on paper, and paper forms are delivered to 201 Johnston Street in St. George.

Yes, once the tax, penalties and collection fees are paid off. Get a payoff from the Delinquent Tax Office ahead of closing and settle with your closing agent how it will be sent.

How long do I have to appeal a Dorchester County assessment?

Ninety days after the assessor mails the notice. Your objection must be written and addressed to the assessor.

Tax business happens in the town of Darlington, even for a house in Hartsville. Plan your errands around that, since all three tax offices share one building.

Who to see for what

The courthouse square address, 1 Public Square, Darlington, SC 29532, houses all three tax offices. Valuation is the Assessor's job, current payments go to the Treasurer, and delinquent accounts belong to the Tax Collector.

  • Treasurer: Room 203, phone 843-398-4160, open weekdays from 8:30 a.m. until 5:00 p.m., closed on holidays.

For a current bill you can pay at the counter, use the drive-thru near the courthouse (8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.), go online through the Tax Search, View and Pay portal, or visit a local bank with your tax notice in hand. Branches in Darlington, Lamar and Hartsville take payments. A check should carry the receipt number.

When taxes turn delinquent

Unpaid tax passes to the Tax Collector on March 17, along with a 15% penalty and added costs. The penalty builds in stages under the statute: 3% after January 15, another 7% by February 2 and another 5% by March 17 (S.C. Code 12-45-180).

Fees pile on top of the penalty in three installments.

DateCost added

How the tax sale works

The December tax sale is held in the Darlington Middle School gymnasium at 150 Pinedale Drive, and bidding opens at 10 a.m. The exact date comes from the Tax Collector at 843-398-4170. The Darlington News and Press carries ads for real property and mobile homes three weeks in a row beforehand.

For the 2026 sale, bidders must finish online registration by December 1, 2026 and pay a $10 nonrefundable fee. Bidder numbers are handed out Saturday, December 5, 2026 at the gymnasium.

  • The owner's last chance to pay a parcel's delinquent tax is 5:00 p.m. the day before; nothing is accepted on sale day.
  • Winning bidders pay in full by 5:00 p.m. the same day, with cash, a cashier's check or a money order.
  • Failing to pay a winning bid brings a $500 fine.
  • Bidders buy at their own risk, because a tax deed is no warranty deed.

Owners keep the right to redeem for 12 months after the sale under S.C. Code 12-51-90. Interest runs from 3% to 12% of the bid, rising the longer they wait. The Tax Collector can give you the final day for a specific parcel.

Every five years the Assessor inspects property under a revaluation plan that the SC Department of Revenue has approved. New construction, renovation or an appraisal review may trigger a visit earlier.

A home occupied by its owner is assessed at 4%, and other property at 6%. To earn the lower ratio, submit a legal residence application after your deed or bond for title is recorded and you move in. Any day before the January 15 penalty date will do. Losing eligibility must be reported within six months. If it is not, the penalty is 100% of the tax paid plus 0.5% interest per month, never less than $30 and never more than that year's tax.

Whoever owns the property on December 31 is named on the bill, and a buyer becomes responsible once a sale becomes final after that date. If you dispute a value, send the Assessor a written objection within 90 days of the mailed notice (S.C. Code 12-60-2510). Selling with back taxes

Owing back tax does not rule out a sale. Your title company will usually pay the balance from the proceeds. Ask the Tax Collector to write out the payoff, because the $20, $40 and $60 steps arrive on set dates and the total moves during the year.

Waiting for the tax sale calendar is risky. Parcels are advertised for three weeks, and the deadline to pay is 5:00 p.m. the day before the auction. If the auction has already happened, the redemption period still lets the owner pay, and a winning bidder does not gain a vested interest right away.

  1. Collect a written payoff from the Tax Collector.
  2. Clear any older delinquent year first, since the office wants it settled before current payments.
  3. Confirm your 4% status with the Assessor.
  4. Warn the title company if a sale date is close.

A cash sale can be timed to close ahead of the auction and does not wait on a buyer's lender, which matters when the last payment day is the afternoon before bidding.

What to have in hand

Darlington sellers do best when they gather records before calling. Bring the tax notice, the receipt number from your last payment and, if you recently bought, proof of the recording date of your deed or bond for title. Those details let the Treasurer and the Tax Collector find your account fast, and they let the Assessor tell you whether a legal residence application is already on file.

If you inherited the house or are selling for a relative, ask each office what proof of authority it wants. A short call to 843-398-4100, the county main line, can point you to the right room in the building. Ask whether copies are fine or originals are needed, and whether the office prefers a visit or a mailed form. Write down the name of anyone who gives you a figure, with the date, so your closing office can follow up.

Where do I pay Darlington County property tax?

Go to the Treasurer in Room 203 at 1 Public Square, Darlington, or use the drive-thru, the online portal or a participating bank. The Treasurer's phone is 843-398-4160. Late bills go to 843-398-4170.

A 15% penalty is added when taxes turn delinquent on March 17, plus $20 in costs. More costs follow: $40 on July 1 and $60 on September 1, for $120 total.

The county sells in December. Bidding starts at 10 a.m. in the Darlington Middle School gymnasium on Pinedale Drive. The date is available at 843-398-4170, and bidder numbers for 2026 are issued Saturday, December 5.

State law allows 12 months, and interest of 3% to 12% of the bid applies depending on timing. The Tax Collector can confirm your parcel's last day.

Due dates and penalties

Late bills climb a ladder. When the house changes hands

A transfer in mid-year can create a trap: the notice went to the old owner, so the new one never saw it. In that situation the penalty must be waived by the treasurer, a rule found in subsection (B) of the penalty statute.

Inherited and newly sold houses are the usual cases. Mail addressed to a person who has died, or to a seller long gone, never finds the current deed holder. Within a week of recording, request an address correction from the treasurer and file your copy of the request.

How to object to your assessment

Put any objection in writing to the assessor. From the mailing of an assessment notice you have 90 days to contest fair market value, special use value, the assessment ratio or the assessment as a whole.

The assessor owes you a notice for a first-time assessment or a rise of $1,000 or more. Without one, a written appeal is open all year. Timing decides the tax year it affects: before the first penalty date, it applies to the current year, and on or after that date, to the next. Absolutely. Before closing, request a written payoff from the treasurer or the delinquent tax office. At the table, the title company subtracts that tax from your proceeds, leaving the buyer a clear record. Since penalties rise in steps, any payoff expires, so find out its last valid date.

Steps to take before closing

Begin with the tax map number, which the treasurer's records and receipts all use. Three questions follow: today's balance, whether this year's bill is settled, and the date each penalty would start. With an open bill, decide with the buyer how it is divided and have the title company note the split.

The buyer then sends both offices a current address. Gather the closing statement, payoff letter and any postmarked receipt in one folder, so a later question about the bill is answered from paper, not memory.

Sellers who are behind gain nothing by waiting. Each added percent increases the very balance you must clear at closing, so request the payoff early and note its good-through date to keep the number steady.

Questions for the treasurer's office

One call can rescue a closing. Learn whether the bill is open, which tax map number carries it, and whether an execution exists. Find out where the notice last went. If the address belongs to a former owner, request a penalty waiver in writing and save the answer.

Next, the assessor: was a changed-value notice sent, and on what date? Your 90 days start at that mailing, and a buyer's lender may want a copy. Planning to object? Ask for the form now, not near the deadline. Phone answers help, but written ones belong in your closing file.

Selling an inherited Aiken County house

Heirs face the tax bill before they face the buyer. Sort out who is receiving the mail first. If the notices still go to the person who died, tell the treasurer where to send them now, and ask in writing for any penalty to be waived if you never saw the notice. Then request a written payoff for every open year.

Gather the deed, the tax map number and your address change request before you list. A buyer's title company will look for open tax, and an unresolved bill slows the sale for everyone. If the house needs work, the tax can still be paid from proceeds at closing, which means you do not have to find the money up front.

Where the value on the assessor's notice looks too high, objecting does not stop the sale. File in writing, keep the mailing date of the notice, and let the title company know an objection is pending so the closing statement reflects it. Ask the assessor how an appeal filed near the January penalty date would apply, since the date decides whether it covers this year or the next.

What a cash sale skips

A sale to a cash buyer drops the lender's appraisal and underwriting, which are often where a closing slips. It does not drop the tax steps. The treasurer still needs to be paid, the penalty calendar still runs, and the title company still wants a payoff letter. What you gain is a shorter list of people who can delay you.

Ninety days from the notice's mailing, in writing. The Aiken County Assessor can name the form.

Yes, if the notice went to the prior owner and none reached you in time. Ask the treasurer in writing.

Beaufort County at a glance

Down in the Lowcountry of southern South Carolina, Beaufort County borders Colleton, Jasper and Hampton counties. Hilton Head and Bluffton lie south of the Broad River and the city of Beaufort and Port Royal lie north of it, and buyers in each half shop differently. Tell the closing attorney early which half your house is in so the right offices are contacted. After closing, the buyer should apply for the 4 percent rate if they will live there.

Checklist for the closing table

On closing day, the closing attorney pulls together the payoff letter, the tax receipt and the settlement statement. Confirm that the payoff covers taxes, penalties and costs through the closing date, and that any open current-year bill is split the way your contract says. Ask for a copy of the final statement that shows the tax payment.

If the sale falls near January 15, check whether the new year's bill has gone out and who will pay it. If it falls after that date, ask whether penalty steps are already adding to the balance. Keep the closing statement, the payoff letter and any receipt with its postmark in one folder, so that a later notice can be answered quickly.

Give the buyer your forwarding address, and tell them to update the mailing address with the Treasurer and the Auditor so future bills reach the right person.

When are Beaufort County, SC property taxes due?

Mid-January, specifically January 15. A payment postmarked later is penalized, so mail early or pay online at myBeaufortCounty.com.

Which office do I call about my Beaufort County tax bill?

The Treasurer, (843) 341-8404, for payment. The Auditor, (843) 255-2500, for notices and homestead. The Assessor, (843) 255-2400, for value or the 4 percent residence rate.

How soon should a Beaufort County buyer apply for the 4 percent rate?

From January 1 of the current year through January 15 of the following year. A home that is not approved is billed at the higher 6 percent rate.

How long do I have to object to a Beaufort County assessment?

Either 90 days from the date of an assessment notice, or from January 1 through January 15 of the following year. The two options cannot be combined in one tax year.

Can I sell a Beaufort County house with tax unpaid?

Yes. Your closing attorney can pay the taxes and penalties from the proceeds, using a payoff from the Treasurer that is good through closing.

A property here might be a town lot in Camden or several acres out toward Lake Wateree.   • Phone the Assessor to find out its hours before driving over.

Because all three are under one roof, one visit can settle a payoff, a legal residence question and a homestead check, as long as you have your parcel information with you.

Penalties and the reassessment cycle

After the due date, state law attaches a penalty, adds more in February and March, and eventually authorizes an execution. The schedule is in Section 12-45-180. Since the amount changes on those dates, ask the Treasurer for this year's figures before you build a closing date around them.

Property is reassessed on the state's five-year cycle. An owner is entitled to a notice whenever value or classification moves by $1,000 or more, so open any letter from the Assessor promptly.

How to appeal your assessment

The first move is a letter to the Assessor, sent within 90 days of the date the notice was mailed. A year with no notice leaves the door open: you may write at any time, and a letter that arrives before the first penalty date counts toward the current tax year.

What follows is a chain of short deadlines. Expect a conference within 30 days of your request, or as soon as practical. Your written protest follows, due 30 days after the meeting, and a written response usually arrives in another 30. Reaching the county Board of Assessment Appeals takes a filing within 30 days of that response. The last rung is a contested case hearing in the Administrative Law Court, which you request within 30 days of the Board's written decision.

A case that is unfinished on December 31 is billed at 80 percent of the protested amount, with the Assessor instructing the auditor. Interest covers the difference once the case ends. Sections 12-60-2510 to 12-60-2550 cover all of it. A notice about the reassessment appeal deadline also appears on the county's home page. Call the Assessor to confirm the window.

The 4 percent legal residence rate

A home you live in is assessed at 4 percent of fair market value, covering up to five contiguous acres, where other property is at 6 percent. File by the first penalty date of the first year you want the rate. Rent the house out for more than 72 days in a calendar year and you lose it.

Your buyer must file a fresh application, because the status does not transfer. Section 12-43-220 penalizes a wrongly held rate at 100 percent of the tax. If a house has sat vacant, expect a buyer's inspector to look hard at the roof, the plumbing and the electrical system, and consider asking the county planning office and your insurer about anything that could come up.

Selling when taxes or title are a problem

Selling with an open tax account is workable. Most sellers go in this order.

Selling right after a reassessment notice? Find out from the Assessor if your appeal window is still open, and let the buyer know about any pending appeal so the next bill holds no surprises.

Dates and steps in a typical sale

A Kershaw County sale usually moves in four stages. First, the title company opens the file and orders the title search, which can run long for an old Camden lot. Second, the payoff is requested from the Treasurer so the county is paid at closing. Third, any open question with the Assessor, such as legal residence status or agricultural classification, is cleared up. Fourth, the deed is signed and recorded, and the deed fee is figured from the value.

The title search is the slowest piece for old lots, and an estate that was never opened is the most common cause of delay. If either applies to you, begin there before anything else. Both buyers and sellers do better with a list of every open item in hand a few weeks before the closing date.

A written objection is due 90 days after the notice is mailed. Once the Assessor replies, 30 days remain to reach the Board of Assessment Appeals.

The Auditor, Room 120. The Assessor takes the 4 percent legal residence and agricultural applications.

On a five-year cycle, as the SC Department of Revenue requires. A notice is also required when value or classification changes by $1,000 or more.

Laurens County in brief

Laurens County sits in the Upstate, inside the Greenville-Anderson-Greer metro area. The city of Laurens serves as the seat and the largest community, and Clinton is the second main town. The 2020 census found 67,539 residents, with about 64 percent in rural areas.

A farmhouse outside Gray Court and a bungalow in town are taxed by the same offices yet attract different buyers. Older housing is common, from mill-era houses to farm property handed down through generations. An inherited house tends to come with an unpaid tax bill, a muddy title or no occupant, and any of these can hold up a closing.

Which office does what

Property tax runs through four county offices, and each answers a different question.

  • Assessor, 864-984-6546: appraises real property and answers legal residence questions.
  • Auditor, 864-984-2535: figures the tax and processes exemption paperwork.
  • Treasurer: takes payments, but neither sets amounts nor keeps owner records.
  • Tax Collector, 864-984-4742: handles accounts still unpaid after the March deadline.

Because the Treasurer holds no owner records, a bill sent to a stale address can go astray. After inheriting or buying a house, notify the Assessor of your address. Rate increases originate with County Council, the school board and municipal councils, which set their own revenue needs, and not with the Treasurer.

Due dates and penalties

Pay by January 15 and no penalty applies. A weekend or holiday on that date extends the deadline to 5:00 p.m. the next business day, and the county must mail bills 30 or more days in advance.

DateWhat happens
January 15Last day to pay without penalty
January 16 onward3 percent penalty (S.C. Code 12-45-180)

March 16Unpaid accounts handed to the Tax Collector

Together they add 15 percent to a bill left until March, before any collection costs. Many troubled accounts on inherited houses began with a bill nobody opened in January.

Challenging your assessment

Write to the Assessor within 90 days of the day the notice went out. You can dispute fair market value, special use value or the assessment ratio.

State law requires a written notice in just two situations, when the Assessor raises a value by $1,000 or more and when a property is assessed for the first time. If none reached you, you may appeal in writing at any time. Filing ahead of the first penalty date applies the appeal to the current tax year, and filing on or after it applies to the next.

The Assessor, 864-984-6546, can give you the form and explain the next step. Before you withhold any payment, ask which balance stays protected while an appeal is open.

The 4 percent and 6 percent rates

Two assessment ratios matter on a Laurens County house. Your own home can be taxed on 4 percent of fair market value if it qualifies as a legal residence. Everything else is taxed on 6 percent, which makes a non-qualifying house one and a half times as costly per dollar of value.

The legal residence ratio comes with strings, found in S.C. Code 12-43-220:

  • You own the house and live in it.
  • You swear, under penalty of perjury, that nobody in your household claims the ratio on another home.
  • You rent it out no more than 72 days in a calendar year.
  • When you sell, the buyer files a new application and you tell the assessor within six months.

Timing is unforgiving. File before the first penalty date of the first year you claim the ratio. A fall closing where the buyer misses that date leaves the house at 6 percent for the year.

Seniors, owners certified totally and permanently disabled and legally blind owners may also qualify for the county homestead exemption, which excludes the first $50,000 of a legal residence's value. Applications go through the Auditor.

Delinquent tax sale and redemption

The Delinquent Tax Collector's office conducts the sale under Chapter 51 of Title 12. After it, the owner keeps a twelve-month right to redeem.

The sale list is published in the Laurens County Advertiser and the Clinton Chronicle. The Forfeited Land Commission gets the opening bid, and bidders must register beforehand and attend in person. A tax deed follows within 45 days once the redemption period ends. Because sale dates change yearly, call 864-984-4742 for the current one.

Interest owed on redemption, set by S.C. Code 12-51-90, is a percentage of the bid that grows each quarter: 3 percent for months 1 to 3, 6 percent for months 4 to 6, 9 percent for months 7 to 9 and 12 percent for months 10 to 12. Those who may redeem are the defaulting owner, the owner's grantee, and a mortgage or judgment creditor.

Taxes when you sell

Closing day is when the year's tax gets paid. The title company takes any open balance out of what the seller would receive. Since penalties shift on set dates, ask the Treasurer or Tax Collector for the exact payoff shortly before you sign.

Sellers in this county keep running into the same few problems:

  • The bill went to a late parent's address and sat unopened.
  • Penalties started January 16 and kept building through March.
  • The legal residence ratio lapsed after a move, and the 6 percent ratio took over.
  • An aging house needs repairs that a lender would not finance.

Someone with a tax debt or a repair list can sell as-is for cash instead. Escrow clears the tax from the proceeds, so you need no money in advance, and with no lender involved there are no repair demands to meet. You can usually pick the closing date. Ask for any payoff figure in writing first.

When you visit an office, carry your deed, newest bill and ID. If the buyer will get next year's bill, ask the Assessor to update the mailing address on the account.

Inherited house checklist

Inherited property tends to raise the same few questions, and each one has a short answer.

  1. Find the tax bills. Check the old address first, because the Treasurer keeps no owner records and mail may have gone there.
  2. Ask the Assessor to correct the address, and ask whether the legal residence ratio is still on the account or lapsed after the owner moved or died.
  3. Call the Tax Collector if the account is delinquent, and ask whether a sale date has been set.
  4. Gather the estate paperwork so the title company can clear the deed.

Once you have all four answers, you know what is owed, who to pay and how much time you have, so choosing between a listing and an as-is cash sale gets easier.

Frequently asked questions

When are Laurens County property taxes due?

Penalty-free through January 15. When that date is a weekend or holiday, you have until 5:00 p.m. the next business day.

Who do I call about a delinquent Laurens County tax bill?

Call the Tax Collector, 864-984-4742. Past-due accounts move to that office after March 16.

Can I appeal my Laurens County assessment?

Yes, by written objection to the Assessor, filed within 90 days of the notice's mailing date. The form is available at 864-984-6546.

Which Laurens County homes are taxed at 4 percent?

A legal residence only. Everything else is at 6 percent, and renting out the home more than 72 days a year can forfeit the lower ratio.

How long can I redeem a Laurens County house after a tax sale?

Twelve months from the sale date under state law. Interest rises from 3 to 12 percent of the bid, depending on which quarter you redeem in.

Due dates and how to pay

Bills for property other than vehicles are due January 15, following a notice that shows up in the fall. S.C. Code 12-45-70 opens the payment window on September 30. A deadline that falls on a weekend or county holiday moves to the next business day. For mail, the postmark date is what counts.

What a late payment costs

Late charges build in three steps under S.C. Code 12-45-180: 3% right after January 15, then 7% more, then 5% more by March 17. Once March 17 is behind you, the treasurer sends an execution to the delinquent tax officer.

The tax sale and your right to redeem

Notice of each sale runs in the Seneca Journal Tribune for three weeks, and only bidders who registered ahead of time may bid. The top bidder wins the property at auction, though the owner keeps one year from the sale date to take it back. The rules sit in S.C. Code Title 12, Chapter 51.

Redeeming is open to the owner, to anyone who got the property from the owner, and to a mortgage or judgment creditor. What redeeming costs is the unpaid taxes and fees plus bid-based interest, and the interest rate steps up every three months:

  • Months 1 to 3: 3%

Legal residence and the 4% rate

The 4% ratio covers your legal residence plus up to five contiguous acres. S.C. Code 12-43-220 puts all other real property at 6%. Once the 4% ratio is granted, the school tax credit for owner-occupied homes follows automatically.

Renting the house out for more than 72 days in a calendar year ends eligibility. Staying silent after eligibility ends is costly: past six months without telling the Assessor, the statute lets the county charge back the full tax paid, plus 0.5% interest monthly, with a $30 floor.

Picture an owner who left town and leased the house for a year. That house will likely carry the 6% rate, and buyers count the higher bill against the price. The Assessor at 864-638-4150 can tell you which rate sits on your parcel today.

Deed recording runs $1.85 for every $500 of value, with $1.30 going to Columbia and $0.55 staying with the county, per S.C. Code 12-24-10 and 12-24-90.

Under 12-43-217 the county revalues property every fifth year. When a value moves by $1,000 or more, the Assessor mails a notice. The next year on the cycle is a question for that office.

At closing the year's taxes are normally prorated between the two sides. A bill that is still open in January should be cleared from the sale money, which keeps penalties away from the next owner.

If you owe taxes and want to sell

Whatever tax is owed gets paid out of your sale money at the closing table. The sellers we hear about in Oconee County tend to fit one of three profiles: heirs holding a house with years of unpaid tax, owners of a lake or hillside place that needs work before a bank will lend, and landlords tired of a rental.

  • Anyone behind: call the Delinquent Tax Office at 864-638-4147 before the sale is advertised.

Hillside and Keowee-side owners often find that the repair list is the real obstacle, not the tax bill. A lender will want the roof, the deck and the shoreline access in good order before it commits, while a cash offer prices the house as it stands.

Who to call

All four counters are at one address, 415 S. Pine St., Walhalla, so one trip can cover several questions. Payments: 864-638-4162. Notices: 864-638-4158. Assessor: 864-638-4150. Delinquent Tax: 864-638-4147. Take the parcel number or address, photo ID and your closing date, if there is one. Ninety days from the date on the notice, in writing, to the Assessor. If no notice was issued that year, you have until January 15 of the next year.

For one year after the sale you can redeem it by paying the taxes, costs and penalties plus 3%, 6%, 9% or 12% interest, depending on the quarter.

When and where to pay

The county Treasurer takes current property tax from October 1 through March 16, though the penalty-free deadline is January 15. Vehicle tax can be paid any time of year. Escrow bills for mortgaged homes are mailed near October 1, and lenders usually pay before the end of December. For mailed checks, the postmark is the payment date.

How to appeal your assessment

A year with a Notice of Valuation gives you 90 days from its mailing to object in writing. A year without one means filing before the first penalty date, which applies to this year's bill, while a later filing applies to next year's.

  1. Informal review: an appraiser examines each appeal filed on time.
  2. Notice of Decision: the result comes by mail from the Assessor.
  3. Board of Assessment Appeals: give the Assessor written notice inside 30 days of the decision date.
  4. Administrative Law Judge Division: the next appeal is due 30 days after the Board's written decision.

Faxed appeals are refused, and the Assessor is the only office that can accept one. Anyone acting for the owner needs a signed authorization or power of attorney. Late or misdirected filings risk dismissal. The Assessor's number is (864) 898-5872.

Reassessment when you sell

Recording a deed can start a fresh valuation, even for a gift. The Assessor's term is Assessable Transfer of Interest, and the new value is fair market value on December 31 of the transfer year. Countywide, the last reassessment took effect December 31, 2018, and appeared on 2019 notices. S.C. Code 12-43-217 calls for reappraisal each fifth year, with a Notice of Valuation whenever a value climbs by $1,000 or more. Phone the Assessor for the next cycle.

The December 31 owner is responsible for that year's tax, and the lien stays with the land. Settle the bill at closing so the buyer starts with a clean slate.

Check your status before listing an estate or a rental. A change from 4% to 6% lifts the bill a buyer will see.

Give the Treasurer your address and ask what is open and what a payoff would be on your target date. Ask the Assessor which rate the house carries and whether a transfer resets the value. Ask Delinquent Tax if any year has been sent over. Date every answer you write down.

Heirs have one more question to ask: is the 4% rate still attached? It may not survive a change of name, and that answer often explains why a buyer's tax estimate comes in above the old bill.

Timeline for a Pickens County sale

Work back from three dates: January 15, February 2 and March 17. Closing ahead of January 15 pays just the base bill, a closing in the next few weeks adds the first penalty, and every later date adds another. Once March 16 has gone by, the account sits with Delinquent Tax and that office supplies the payoff.

Request the payoff when the contract is signed instead of the day before closing. An outdated figure can hold up funding. Hand the title company both office numbers so it can verify directly.

Since the year's tax follows the December 31 owner, the family should agree on who pays before the deed is recorded. A brief note to the title company on how the bill will be split avoids arguments at the table.

Object in writing to the Assessor within 90 days of the Notice of Valuation. A decision can be taken to the Board of Assessment Appeals within 30 days, then to the Administrative Law Judge Division.

County government is at 129 Screven Street, Georgetown, SC 29442. Write to P.O. Box 421270, Georgetown, SC 29442-4200, or call the main number, 843-545-3063.

Most long-held properties are capped at a 15 percent rise over the prior value. Exceptions include homes sold or transferred in the previous year, new construction or additions and newly added parcels. A capped property shows two values on its notice. A millage rollback is also mandatory, so reassessment cannot bring the county extra revenue. The county says the effect on taxpayers overall is little to none, although an individual bill can change.

  • Primary residence: ask the Assessor for the 4 percent rate.
  • Homestead exemption: owners 65 or older may apply to the Auditor to exempt up to $50,000 of value.
  • ATI exemption: buyers of rentals or commercial property may ask the Auditor to cut the assessed value increase caused by a change of ownership by up to 25 percent.

How to appeal a Georgetown County value

A written objection is due within 90 days of the notice date. An informal appeal form comes with the notice, and an appraiser in the Assessor's Office reviews it. You do not need to hire an appraiser, filing is free and you may attach recent appraisals or sales data.

Still unhappy? Request a hearing at the Board of Assessment Appeals, and after that the South Carolina Administrative Law Court. An appeal does not hold up the tax bill, so pay on time and avoid penalties.

Interest is 3 percent in months one to three, 6 percent in months four to six, 9 percent in months seven to nine and 12 percent in the last three months, never above the forfeited land commission's bid. A tax deed is not a warranty deed, and the county tells buyers to talk to an attorney.

Before you list

Georgetown sellers can save time by gathering a few records. Start with the latest tax bill, which shows the stormwater fee and whether the 4 percent rate is in place. Add the 2025 reassessment notice, since it shows the capped and uncapped values and tells a buyer what to expect. If you own a rental or commercial property and just bought it, ask the Auditor about the ATI exemption.

Then deal with the physical side of a coastal house. Buyers ask about flood zones, roof age and storm repairs, so a folder with those records speeds up the conversation. Offices rely on you to report address changes, so confirm that the Assessor and the Auditor both have the right mailing address before closing.

Selling a Georgetown County house with taxes due

If your parcel could be on the sale list, ask the Delinquent Tax Department what is owed today. A seller with a balance can generally still close, and the title company pays the taxes, penalties and any stormwater fee from the proceeds.

January 15, under state law. Penalties then begin at 3 percent, add 7 percent after February 1 and add 5 percent after March 16.

Yes, it appears as a line on the property tax bill, with the same due date as the taxes.

Ninety days from the notice date. Use the form that arrives with the notice, and the Assessor's Office reviews it at no cost.

It is on Monday, December 7, 2026, with bidding at 10:00 a.m. in County Council Chambers at 129 Screven Street. Sign up by noon on December 4.

Does a Georgetown County reassessment mean my taxes go up?

Not necessarily. The county rolls the millage back when values rise, so some bills go up, some fall, and the total collected stays about the same.

Colleton County in brief

Walterboro anchors Colleton County, a big, wet slice of the Lowcountry covering 1,133.28 square miles, 1,056.50 of them land. Three rivers, the Edisto, the Salkehatchie and the Ashepoo, cross it, and protected ground such as Bear Island and Donnelley takes up a fair share of the map.
