Retail, health care and food service provide most jobs, and Colleton County School District, Cracker Barrel, Food Lion and Walmart are among the bigger employers.

Which office does what

Colleton splits tax work across three desks. The Assessor puts a value on property. The Auditor turns that value into a tax figure. The Treasurer takes the payment. Land and building records live with the Assessor, and personal property and vehicle records live with the Auditor, so an address correction must reach the right one.

Due dates and penalties

Colleton follows S.C. Code 12-45-180 for late charges. Unpaid at January 16 (or 30 days after notices go out, whichever is later), a bill gains 3%. By February 2 it gains 7% more, and by March 17 another 5%.

If anything is still owed on March 17, the county treasurer hands an execution to the officer who collects delinquent tax. For mailed checks, the U.S. postmark is the test of timeliness.

The December 31 owner of record is the one named on the bill. A house that closes after December 31 leaves the next year's tax with the buyer. Ask the Treasurer for a billing and payoff figure so no stray balance surprises you at the table.

Reassessment, the 4% rate and appeals

The 4% ratio goes to owner-occupied primary residences. All other property is assessed at 6%. Submit a legal residence application to the Assessor before January 15. Owner-occupied primary homes qualify, and any change in use must be reported within six months.

How often the county reassesses

An assessment notice is not a tax bill. Notices mostly arrive in the year after a value change, a corrected error, a transfer or a countywide reassessment. The Assessor can tell you the next cycle year.

Selling can trigger a separate reassessment, which the county labels an Assessable Transfer of Interest. It takes effect December 31 of the year the deed was conveyed. How to appeal your assessment

Appeals must be written and filed within 90 days of the assessment notice. With no notice that year, the cutoff moves to January 15, matching the first penalty date on the tax notice.

Legal residence and the 4% rate

Owners who occupy their home may apply for the 4% legal residence rate, using a form on the Assessor's website. Under S.C. Code 12-43-220, other real property is assessed at 6%.

Rural parcels need extra care. For a family-owned house, start with the Assessor at 803-533-6220 to confirm who is the owner of record, where bills go and which rate applies. The mailing address for correspondence is P.O. Box 9000 in Orangeburg.

Estates often sit for a year or more, and taxes keep coming due on January 15 whether or not the title is settled. Compare the unpaid balance with the likely price early, so the family knows what will be left after the county is paid.

What to bring and how to prepare

Take the property address or parcel details, photo ID and, for an estate, proof that you may act for the owner. Visit the Assessor at 1437 Amelia Street or call 803-533-6220. The Delinquent Tax Collector's counter keeps weekday hours from 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

Timing a sale around the January and March dates

Two dates drive most decisions here. January 15 is the due date and the cutoff for appeals when no notice was mailed. March 17 is when unpaid real property taxes turn delinquent. A sale that closes ahead of the first date is simplest, since the payoff is just the base bill.

If you list in late winter, expect penalties to be part of the payoff. That is manageable when the price is well above the debt. When it is not, call the Delinquent Tax Collector early and ask what the county needs to release the parcel at closing.

Jasper County in brief

Jasper County is South Carolina's southernmost county, in the Lowcountry, with Ridgeland as the seat and Hardeeville as the largest community. Population rose from 20,678 in 2000 to 28,791 in 2020, and the 2025 estimate is 38,533. Most of the recent growth is around Hardeeville, where planned communities along U.S. 278 and Argent Boulevard, including Sun City Hilton Head, added thousands of residents. The city went from 2,952 people in 2010 to 7,473 in 2020, with 16,459 estimated for 2025.

That growth brought a larger tax base and many new buyers, but also plenty of older family land, and the two kinds of property are handled quite differently when they are sold.

Which office does what

Three county offices split the work. Values and appeals belong to the Assessor, bills and vehicles to the Auditor, and payments to the Treasurer. Accounts that fall behind become the Delinquent Tax Collector's responsibility. You will find all of them at 358 Third Avenue, Ridgeland, SC 29936.

Due dates and penalties

January 15 is the last day to pay without penalty. For 2026 taxes paid in 2027, the Treasurer lists these dates:

Pay byPenalty startsTotal penalty
January 15, 2027January 16, 20273%

March 17 is the handoff to the Delinquent Tax Collector. State law stacks the penalty: an initial charge, a second layer on February 2, a third on March 17, then an execution. Two exceptions exist. The treasurer may forgive a penalty if a mailed payment got the wrong postmark. The treasurer must forgive it if the house was sold, the bill went to the former owner, and the buyer never received a notice in time. Section 12-45-180 has the exact wording.

Delinquent taxes and the tax sale

If real property stays unpaid, it can go to a tax sale, and the former owner then has a 12-month redemption period. The timeline the county posts under Section 12-51-40 is as follows.

  • March 17: the account is delinquent.
  • April 1: delinquent notices go out by mail.
  • Normally September: certified notices are sent on delinquent real estate and mobile homes.
  • Three Wednesdays in a row ahead of the sale: an advertisement runs in a local paper.
  • First Monday of November: the sale takes place at the Government Building, 358 Third Avenue, Ridgeland.

After the auction, anyone with a stake in the title can buy the property back by covering the taxes and sale costs inside the year: the owner, a mortgage company or a grantee. That is the outer limit for any plan to keep or sell the house. A closing ahead of the first Monday of November lets the proceeds pay the back taxes.

How to appeal your assessment

The whole process runs on paper and begins with the Assessor, and the clock is 90 days from the mailing date of your notice. The county's Assessor Appeals page and Sections 12-60-2510 to 12-60-2550 of the state code describe the stages.

  1. Request a conference from the Assessor in writing. Expect it to be set roughly a month out, and know that skipping it ends your appeal rights for that year.
  2. If the conference does not settle it, put a protest in writing, due 30 days after the conference or the Assessor's Notice of Action. Include contact details, a property description, your reasons, and the value and classification you think are right.
  3. The Assessor mails a written reply, normally about a month later.
  4. The next stop is the county Board of Assessment Appeals, and you get 30 days from that reply. Miss it and the new value is final.
  5. Both sides exchange evidence 15 days or more before the Board conference, with replies due 7 days or more before it.
  6. The last step is a contested case hearing at the Administrative Law Court, requested no later than 30 days after the Board puts its decision in writing.

In a year when no notice was mailed, an appeal can be filed whenever you like. If it goes in before January 15, it covers that tax year, and from January 15 on it covers the following year. An attorney, CPA, fiduciary or appraiser may act for you, provided the authorization names one specific person.

If the dispute is still alive at year end, the bill is issued at 80 percent of the protested amount, and any difference is settled afterward with interest.

The 4 percent legal residence rate

A house you live in, together with as many as five contiguous acres, is taxed on 4 percent of fair market value. The application is due by the first penalty date in your first claim year. More than 72 rental days in one calendar year disqualifies the home.

A wrongful claim costs a penalty equal to the whole tax paid, plus interest, and the county keeps a page for reporting residential exemption fraud. Farm acreage can earn a 4 percent rate as well. If that land changes use, rollback taxes cover the current year and the three years before. The rules are in Chapter 43 of Title 12.

Permits and past work

A new roof, an addition, and electrical, plumbing or heating work all require a Jasper County building permit. Buyers and inspectors ask about this, so find out whether past work on your house was permitted before you list it. The Planning and Building office is at 358 Third Avenue, Room 202, phone (843) 717-3650. Report code violations to (843) 547-8290.

Utility service is another thing buyers ask about. Power comes from Palmetto Electric Cooperative or Dominion Energy, and water and sewer from the Town of Ridgeland or the Beaufort-Jasper Water and Sewer Authority.

  • Easement: $25 plus stamps.

The state deed fee is $1.85 per $500 of value under Title 12, Chapter 24. The register's office is at 358 Third Avenue, and its mailing box number should be confirmed by phone before you send anything.

Selling with back taxes

A tax debt is no barrier to selling. Obtain a payoff from the Treasurer or Tax Collector and pass it to the title company, which settles with the county before you are paid.

When the account is already delinquent, aim to close before the first Monday of November. After the sale, the clock for redemption runs 12 months. A buyer paying cash can move faster than one waiting on a loan, which helps when time is short.

For a family property, check who is on the recorded deed, and have estate documents ready if an owner has died. Questions about whether earlier work was permitted can go to the Planning and Building office.

January 15. The Treasurer lists a 3 percent penalty from January 16, 10 percent from February 2 and 15 percent from March 17, and then files go to the Delinquent Tax Collector.

Who takes appeals of a Jasper County assessment?

The Assessor, at the appeals line (843) 717-3620. Your written objection is due 90 days after the notice was mailed.

What is the redemption period after a Jasper County tax sale?

One year from the date of the sale. Paying the overdue taxes and costs within that year lets the owner, a mortgage company or a grantee take the property back.

Where and when is the Jasper County tax sale held?

It takes place the first Monday of November at 358 Third Avenue, Ridgeland. The newspaper ad gives the date and time.

Lancaster County in brief

Lancaster County hugs the North Carolina border in the Piedmont and is part of the Charlotte metro area. The City of Lancaster is the seat. Up in the northern panhandle, Indian Land is a big unincorporated community of 32,759 people (2020). Countywide, the 2020 census found 96,016 residents, and the 2025 estimate is 114,296.

A new house in the growing north and an older house on acreage elsewhere in the county attract different buyers, yet both are taxed and recorded through the same handful of county offices.

Who collects property tax

Current taxes are the County Treasurer's job, handled at the County Administration Building, 101 North Main Street, Lancaster. When real property is still unpaid after the March deadline, the Tax Collector's Office takes it over.

Due dates and penalties

No penalty applies to real estate or personal property tax paid by January 15. Should the 15th be a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, you have until 5 pm on the following business day. Bills reach mailboxes at least 30 days ahead.

March 16 is the handoff date to the Tax Collector's Office for anything still owed, adjusted when it lands on a weekend or holiday. Vehicle bills run separately and come due at month end, mailed a month in advance.

State law sets the penalty rates: one charge once the due date passes, with more added in February and again in March. See Section 12-45-180. It also makes the postmark the test for a mailed payment. Phone the Treasurer for the dollar amounts on your own bill.

Appealing an assessment

Everything starts with a letter to the County Assessor, mailed within 90 days of the notice date. State law sets the stages that follow.

  1. Ask the Assessor for a conference, which should be scheduled within a month.
  2. After the conference, you have 30 days to file a written protest.
  3. The Assessor answers in writing, normally within 30 days.
  4. Take the dispute to the county board no later than 30 days after that answer.
  5. Within 30 days of the board's decision you can ask the Administrative Law Court for a contested case hearing.

A case that is unfinished on December 31 is billed at 80 percent of the protested value until it ends. Sections 12-60-2510 to 12-60-2550 hold the full text. A separate rule, Section 12-43-217, puts counties on a five-year reappraisal cycle and requires notice to owners when value or class moves by $1,000 or more.

The 4 percent legal residence rate

Where the owner lives in the house, 4 percent of fair market value is the taxable amount, and up to five contiguous acres come along with it. The application must reach the county by the first penalty date of your first claim year. More than 72 rental days in a year ends eligibility.

After you sell, the buyer applies on their own. An improper claim costs 100 percent of the tax paid, plus interest. Farm land can get 4 percent too, but a switch in use brings rollback taxes for this year and the three before. Chapter 43 of Title 12 has the details.

Indian Land

Indian Land has no downtown and lies about six miles east of Fort Mill. U.S. 521 and SC 160 are its main roads, and no public transportation serves it. A 2014 overlay district sets design rules for new construction along those corridors.

  • Tax Collector: past-due real property after the March deadline.
  • Assessor: value, classification and appeals.
  • Development Services: permits and land use.

Permit and zoning questions are answered by the county's Code of Ordinances, which is posted on the county site. Foreclosure and deed in lieu transfers to a mortgage holder are exempt, per Title 12, Chapter 24.

Selling with unpaid taxes

Overdue taxes slow a sale without stopping it. A workable sequence:

  2. Request a payoff valid through the date you expect to close, because the amount moves on penalty dates.
  3. Ask the Assessor whether the parcel has the 4 percent rate or an agricultural classification.
  4. Hand the figure to the title company, which settles with the county out of your proceeds.

Paying cash and buying as-is lets a buyer skip the lender appraisal, so timing depends mostly on title work and the payoff. An inherited house needs its estate paperwork in order, which closing agents normally request up front.

Plan on a few phone calls rather than a trip downtown. Almost every question on this page can be answered by one of the numbers listed above, and the Treasurer accepts payment by phone.

What to have ready for closing

Preparation saves time. Round up the deed or tax map number, the newest tax bill and a photo ID before contacting an office. If the account is behind, write down the payoff figure along with the date it was quoted. Penalties step up on fixed dates, so a figure from January will not match one from March.

Confirm that your legal residence application is on file, and let the buyer know they must file their own. At 101 N Main Street in Lancaster, on the web at lancastersctax.qpaybill.com, by phone at 803-797-2853, or by mail to P.O. Box 729, Lancaster, SC 29720.

To the Tax Collector's Office, 803-283-8885. Get a payoff figure there before closing.

Yes. A 2.35 percent convenience fee applies and goes to the service provider rather than the county. A returned payment is $30.

Greenwood County in brief

Greenwood County lies in the western Piedmont of South Carolina, with the city of Greenwood as seat and largest community. Hodges, Ninety Six, Troy and Ware Shoals are the other incorporated places. The 2020 Census counted 69,351 residents, nearly the same as 69,661 in 2010, and the 2025 estimate is 70,379.

Growth here has been slow and steady, so many houses stay with one family for decades and pass to heirs. An heir who does not plan to keep the property often finds a cash sale simpler than a listing. Lake Greenwood adds a layer of second homes, which are taxed differently from a primary residence (more on that below).

Offices and phone numbers

Three offices in the Greenwood County Courthouse, 528 Monument Street, deal with property tax. Each is open 7:45 to 5:30 Monday through Thursday and closed on Friday.

OfficeRoomPhoneWhat it handles
Assessor109(864) 942-8537Valuation and appeals
AuditorSuite 107(864) 942-8543Homestead and legal residence credit

One rule trips people up. An appeal must challenge value, use classification or ratio. Complaining that the bill is too big is not a valid appeal, so take that to the Assessor with a specific reason.

Payment schedule and penalties

Real estate tax here can be spread out. Advance installments are due in February, April, June, August and October, with the balance owed by January 15 of the following year.

  • Options for paying: the counter, the mail, the lobby drop box, or the county's online vendor.
  • Cash, certified checks, money orders and the major credit cards are accepted, and card payments may include a convenience fee.
  • A check drawn on an out-of-state bank will be refused for delinquent real estate tax.

Penalties follow S.C. Code 12-45-180: 3 percent once January 15 passes, 7 percent more on February 2, and 5 percent more on March 17. The Tax Collector can tell you the exact total on your own bill.

Homestead exemption and the school-tax credit

Three groups can apply for the homestead exemption: owners 65 or older, owners who are totally and permanently disabled, and owners who are legally blind. They need fee simple title or a life estate in their primary home, plus a full calendar year of South Carolina residency as of December 31 of the preceding tax year.

Legal residents also receive a 4 percent homeowners credit against school operating taxes, leaving only the school bond portion to pay. That credit stops short of second homes, land and business property. A lake cottage you do not live in full time is billed on a different basis than your main house, and the Assessor can confirm how your parcel is classified.

Report any sale, rental or deed change to the Auditor. At a sale the seller's exemption simply ends, and the buyer files a separate application.

How to appeal your assessment

Object in writing within 90 days of the mailing date when the notice raised value by $1,000 or more, as S.C. Code 12-60-2510 provides. The letter goes to the Assessor in Room 109.

Keep the letter to the point: name the parcel, say what value or classification you think is right, and give your reasons, whether that is a recent comparable sale or a condition problem the appraisal missed.

Farm land, rollback taxes and new construction

Agricultural-use classification calls for at least 5 acres in timber or 10 acres in crops, and pasture counts as crops. When the use changes, up to five years of taxes can come due. That is a real issue for anyone dividing a family tract before a sale, so ask the Assessor before you sign a contract.

Builders can seek an exemption on newly built single-family homes, and subdivision lots may qualify for a multiple lot discount. Both go through the Assessor.

Recording a deed and redeeming after a tax sale

The Register of Deeds is in Room 114 of the courthouse, phone (864) 942-8612, open 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Monday through Friday. Documents delivered before 4 p.m. are recorded that day, later ones wait until the next day, and originals come back by mail 3 to 5 business days afterward.

The recording tax is $1.85 per $500 under Title 12, Chapter 24. State tax liens no longer get filed with county offices. They show up on the Department of Revenue's registry instead.

Redemptions after a tax sale go through Room 101 and are accepted as cash, certified check or money order only. Cards are not taken. Selling before the sale lets you skip that step altogether.

Selling a Greenwood County house with tax or title issues

Most sellers work through the same short list.

  1. Ask the Tax Collector what is still owed, remembering that advance installments already paid count toward the year.
  2. Find out from the Auditor whether the account carries a homestead exemption or school-tax credit, and report the pending sale.
  3. If the land is classified as agricultural and you are splitting it, ask the Assessor what rollback tax might result.
  4. Get the recorded deed from the Register of Deeds and make sure the name on it is the seller's. Inherited property needs estate paperwork in order before closing.

The three tax offices and the Register of Deeds share one building, so one trip can cover every stop, as long as you avoid Friday for the tax offices. A cash buyer purchasing as-is has no lender appraisal to wait for, so you pick the closing date around your own plans.

Timing a sale around the tax year

Selling in the first weeks of the year deserves care. Between January 15 and March 17 the penalties step up, and a payoff quoted early in that stretch will be higher by the time you close. Ask for a new figure once the closing date is set.

If you already paid advance installments in February, April or June, your title agent should credit them against the balance. Bring those receipts to the closing table.

For a house nobody lives in, the main risk is an unopened bill. A bill that goes unnoticed does not stop penalties, and a tax sale can follow. An heir who sorts out the account early has more choices, including selling before the Tax Collector's office handles redemptions.

Whichever way the sale goes, keep your copies of the deed, the final tax receipt and any letter from the Auditor about the homestead exemption. Buyers and title companies often ask for them.

By January 15 of the year following the tax year. Advance installments are possible in February, April, June, August and October.

Can I pay Greenwood County taxes over the internet?

Yes. The county's payment vendor handles current and delinquent real, personal and mobile home taxes, and you can also pay at the counter, by mail or in the lobby drop box. Cards may carry a fee.

Who is eligible for homestead in Greenwood County?

Owners 65 or older, totally and permanently disabled, or legally blind, who also meet the ownership and residency tests. File in person with the Auditor and report a sale or rental.

How long is the window to object to my Greenwood County value?

Ninety days after the mailing of a notice that raised value by $1,000 or more. Send the written objection to the Assessor's office.

The Assessor, Auditor and Tax Collector run 7:45 to 5:30 Monday through Thursday and are closed Friday. The Register of Deeds is open 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Monday through Friday.

Williamsburg County at a glance

This Pee Dee county covers about 937 square miles, almost entirely land. Kingstree serves as county seat and largest community, with Andrews, Greeleyville, Hemingway, Lane and Stuckey nearby. Manufacturing supplies the largest share of jobs, at about 30.2 percent, with public administration, retail and health care behind it. Interstates 20, 26 and 95 connect the county to larger southeastern cities.

Homes left by a parent and never retitled turn up often. Estate papers will be requested before a deed can go on record.

Storms and the Black River

Ground along the Black River can flood in a big storm, so check the flood zone before marketing a home. Hurricane Matthew in October 2016 dropped close to 10 inches of rain on parts of the county, with one gauge northwest of Kingstree reading 13.70 inches.

Storm damage makes conventional financing difficult. Selling for cash in present condition is an option for owners who can't pay for repairs.

Offices and phone numbers

Your bill passes through four hands: the assessor values the property, the auditor applies the millage, the treasurer collects payment, and the delinquent tax collector steps in after March 16. All four answer at the county switchboard, (843) 355-9321.

Due dates and penalties

Pay by January 15 and nothing extra is added. Miss it and 3 percent goes on the bill. From February 2 through March 16, another 7 percent is stacked on top. On March 17 the account moves to the delinquent tax collector, where unpaid real property and mobile home bills go into execution, and state law attaches a final 5 percent.

The 3 percent step begins on whichever comes later: January 16, or thirty days after the notices were mailed. That gives some relief when the county mails late.

Assessment and how to appeal

Fair market value is multiplied by 4 percent for the home you live in and by 6 percent for most everything else. If you inherit a house, move out and rent it, expect the higher rate and a larger bill. Vacant lots are in the 6 percent group as well.

Values are redone every five years, though an ordinance can let a county hold the new numbers back for one tax year. You should hear from the county whenever your value or classification shifts by $1,000 or more.

Disputes move through four stages, and each has its own deadline:

  1. A written objection to the assessor, within 90 days of the mailing date on the notice.
  2. A written protest, within 30 days after you meet with the assessor.
  3. An appeal to the county board of assessment appeals, within 30 days of the assessor's reply.
  4. A hearing request to the Administrative Law Court, within 30 days of the board's written ruling.

No notice came this year? You may still object in writing, and one filed ahead of the first penalty date applies to that year's bill.

If the tax goes unpaid

The path from a late bill to a lost house is slow, and it has several warning points. Around April 1 the officer mails a delinquent notice to the taxpayer and anyone who holds the land by grant. If 30 days pass with no payment, the officer seizes the real property by certified mail. Then the property is advertised as a Delinquent Tax Sale, once weekly for three weeks, before it is sold.

Even after the sale you have twelve months to get it back. The owner, a grantee, or a mortgage or judgment creditor may redeem. The price is the bid plus interest on it that grows by quarter: 3 percent in months one through three, then 6, 9 and 12 percent. About 20 to 45 days before the window closes, the collector mails a certified notice. For this year's sale schedule and fee amounts, call extension 5800.

Rural parcels bring their own questions. A mobile home on the land is billed under the same schedule as the land. Pull every tax notice for the property, not just the one for the house, and confirm that each is paid or accounted for.

If a family farm parcel passed down without a clean title, start the estate paperwork early, since the deed can't be recorded until it is sorted. Walk the boundaries with someone who knows them, note anything that floods near the Black River, and write down repairs you won't make. A buyer who knows these facts up front is far less likely to renegotiate later.

Deed transfer costs

Recording a deed runs $1.85 for every $500 of value, or part of $500, and by default the seller pays. The state keeps $1.30 and the county gets $0.55.

An affidavit has to go with the deed, either stating what the property is worth or explaining why the deed is exempt. Transfers of $100 or less and deeds in lieu of foreclosure are exempt. Lying on the affidavit is a misdemeanor.

Selling with taxes due

Nothing says you must clear the bill before you sell. The closing attorney requests a payoff from the treasurer or the delinquent office and takes that amount out of your proceeds, so a sale ahead of a tax sale can wipe out the debt.

Ask for the payoff on paper, with penalties and costs included, and find out how many days it holds. Inherited houses call for a death certificate and any probate papers. Mention a mobile home on the land to the buyer, because its tax runs on the same schedule. When a tax sale has already taken place, the twelve months to redeem count from the sale date.

Payment is penalty-free through January 15. A 3 percent charge follows, with another 7 percent from February 2 through March 16.

Call (843) 355-9321 and ask for extension 5900 for the treasurer, 5600 for the auditor, 5500 for the assessor or 5800 for the delinquent tax collector.

How long do I have to appeal a Williamsburg County assessment?

Ninety days, counted from the mailing date of the assessor's notice, to file a written objection. Each later step has a 30 day limit.

Can I sell my Williamsburg County house if the tax is delinquent?

Yes, and the balance usually comes out of the proceeds at closing. First obtain a written payoff from the delinquent tax office so it covers penalties and costs.

Can I get my house back after a Williamsburg County tax sale?

Yes, if you act inside twelve months. Redeeming means paying the winning bid plus 3, 6, 9 or 12 percent interest, depending on the quarter. A grantee or a mortgage or judgment creditor may redeem too.

Union County in brief

Union County takes up about 515 square miles in the upstate and shares borders with Cherokee, York, Chester, Fairfield, Newberry, Laurens and Spartanburg counties. A slice of Sumter National Forest sits within it. Its seat is the city of Union, home to 8,174 people in 2020.

Health care is now the biggest employment sector, at about 21.7 percent. Milliken & Company, Sonoco, Walmart, Timken and Dollar General rank among the big employers. Textile plants once dominated, then mostly closed or moved overseas during the 1980s and 1990s.

Older neighborhoods and old family land

Three areas are on the National Register of Historic Places: East Main Street-Douglass Heights, South Street-South Church Street, and Union Downtown. An owner inside one should phone the county before starting outside work, to learn whether local rules apply.

Plenty of land here stays in one family for generations, and county lines have shifted more than once, with two townships going to Cherokee County in 1897. Old deeds may name places and neighbors long gone. On inherited acreage, a title company should check where the records sit and who is entitled to sign before a contract is signed.

Reappraisal and your valuation notice

The 2025 countywide reappraisal values property as of December 31, 2024, and the 2024 taxable value carries forward for four more years, barring a few listed exceptions. State law calls for a new reappraisal every five years.

  • That valuation and classification notice is not a tax bill.
  • Any shift of $1,000 or more in value or classification must be reported to you by the county.
  • Mill levies are set annually, so your bill can move even when assessed value stays flat.
  • A missing tax notice doesn't change the tax, penalty, interest, due date or lien.

Send the Assessor your up-to-date mailing address in writing. Agricultural land switched to another use triggers rollback taxes covering this year and the three before.

How to appeal your assessment

Filing inside 90 days of the notice date preserves all your options. The back of the valuation notice and the Assessor's website explain the steps, and an informal appeal form is online.

County Council appoints the Board of Assessment Appeals, which holds conferences on classification and real property assessment. Setting values or taxes is not its job. Its ruling can be contested by the owner or the Assessor before the Administrative Law Judge Division, with the S.C. Supreme Court as a last stop.

Filing an appeal won't stretch your payment deadline, so pay on schedule to avoid penalties and interest.

Due dates and how to pay

The county's bills trail the tax year by twelve months. October brings the notices, and a payment made through January 15 is penalty-free. Later payments add 3 percent, then 10 percent after February 1, then 15 percent plus execution costs after March 16. A bill is delinquent from March 17, or the next business day.

Walk-in payers may use cash, cashier's checks, postal money orders, certified checks or Visa and Mastercard. Mail, phone and lockbox payments are taken as well. Delinquent bills can't be paid in pieces, because the county's system can't record partial payments.

South Carolina law backs the same stepped penalty and allows the treasurer to waive it for a taxpayer with clear and convincing proof of paying on time.

The tax sale

Parcels with unpaid taxes are auctioned in public. Anyone hoping to keep a parcel must pay before the auction, since paying later does not undo it. A sale takes place each fall; call (864) 429-1617 for the next date, how to register and what happened at the last one.

  • The Union County News carries the notice for three consecutive weeks ahead of the sale.
  • Parcels without a buyer pass to the Union County Forfeited Land Commission, which hands them out first come, first served, for cash.
  • An owner can buy a sold parcel back by paying taxes, assessments, penalties and costs, with 3, 6, 9 or 12 percent interest added.

The state's redemption window is 12 months. Ask the office how that clock applies to your parcel.

Selling with taxes owed

Begin with a payoff letter that includes penalties, from the Treasurer or the Delinquent Tax Collector. Check the tax map number and the recorded owner ahead of closing. A notice mailed to the previous owner may qualify for a waiver under state law, so ask. Old family land warrants a title search.

The closing agent subtracts what is owed from your proceeds, which lets the buyer take the property without the tax lien. Learn the figure early and the last week stays calm. If a sale date is near, say so to any buyer immediately.

Putting it together before you sell

A sale in Union County usually runs in this order. First, learn what is owed by calling the Treasurer or the Delinquent Tax Collector. Second, find out whether a valuation notice recently changed your value or classification, since a wrong figure can be appealed inside the 90-day window. Third, settle who must sign, which matters most with inherited houses. Fourth, agree on a buyer and a closing date, and let the closing agent pay off the tax from your proceeds.

Documents worth having on hand

Before phoning or visiting, set out the tax map number, the latest bill and any valuation notice, plus a photo ID. To claim a homestead exemption, ask the Auditor which proof is required. An appeal is stronger with evidence of value, like recent sales nearby. Copies of every filing, with dates, are worth keeping.

Frequently asked questions

When are Union County property taxes due?

Penalty-free through January 15. After that the charge becomes 3 percent, then 10 percent after February 1, and 15 percent plus execution costs after March 16.

How long do I have to appeal a Union County assessment?

Ninety days from the notice date. Appealing does not push back the due date.

Does Union County accept partial payments on delinquent taxes?

No. Its bookkeeping system can't take partial payments, so the whole delinquent amount is required.

Who do I call about Union County property tax?

Values: Assessor, (864) 429-1650. Bills and exemptions: Auditor, (864) 429-1618. Payments: Treasurer, (864) 429-1606. Overdue taxes: Delinquent Tax Collector, (864) 429-1617.

Can I still redeem a property after a Union County tax sale?

Yes, inside the redemption window. You owe the taxes, assessments, penalties and costs, plus interest of 3, 6, 9 or 12 percent based on timing.
